html:
The discovery, in December 1938 in Berlin, that a uranium atom hit by a neutron can split in two, releasing a great deal of energy. It opened the road to both nuclear power and the atomic bomb.

The chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann were firing neutrons at uranium and found barium among the products, a much lighter element. They could not explain it. Hahn's longtime partner, the physicist Lise Meitner, had fled Nazi Germany for Sweden that year because she was of Jewish descent. Over Christmas she and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out that the nucleus had split, used Einstein's formula to estimate the energy, and named the process fission.

Scientists soon saw that each split released more neutrons, so a chain reaction was possible. In 1939 Albert Einstein signed a letter warning President Roosevelt that Germany might build a bomb. This led to the Manhattan Project and the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.

Hahn alone received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery, and Meitner's part was long overlooked.
